1	# Orva
2	
3	[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/Harsh-2002/Orva?style=flat-square&label=release&color=7c5cbf)](https://github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/releases/latest)
4	[![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/docker-ghcr.io%2Fharsh--2002%2Forva-2496ED?style=flat-square&logo=docker&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/pkgs/container/orva)
5	[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache%202.0-green?style=flat-square)](LICENSE)
6	[![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-1.26+-00ADD8?style=flat-square&logo=go&logoColor=white)](https://go.dev)
7	[![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-24-339933?style=flat-square&logo=node.js&logoColor=white)](https://nodejs.org)
8	[![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.14-3776AB?style=flat-square&logo=python&logoColor=white)](https://python.org)
9	
10	**Self-hosted Functions-as-a-Service for your homelab or on-prem server.**
11	
12	Write a JavaScript, TypeScript, or Python function, hit deploy — Orva runs it in an
13	isolated nsjail sandbox and serves it over HTTP. One Docker container gives you the
14	runtime, a dashboard, a CLI, an MCP server, and a built-in AI assistant. It's for the
15	Lambda/Workers workflow — write a function, invoke it over HTTP, schedule it, chain it —
16	on hardware you control (a Pi, a homelab box, a VPS, bare metal). No cloud account, no
17	per-invocation billing.
18	
19	> **Active development.** Solid for homelabs, side-projects, and internal tools.
20	> Not recommended for customer-facing production yet.
21	
22	---
23	
24	## Quick start
25	
26	```bash
27	docker run -d --name orva -p 8443:8443 \
28	  --pid host --cgroupns host \
29	  --cap-add SYS_ADMIN --cap-add NET_ADMIN \
30	  --security-opt seccomp=unconfined \
31	  --security-opt apparmor=unconfined \
32	  --security-opt systempaths=unconfined \
33	  --device /dev/net/tun \
34	  -v orva-data:/var/lib/orva \
35	  -v /sys/fs/cgroup:/sys/fs/cgroup:rw \
36	  ghcr.io/harsh-2002/orva:latest
37	```
38	
39	> `--pid host` and `--cgroupns host` are **required** on the default runc runtime:
40	> nsjail enrolls each sandbox PID in the host cgroup hierarchy, and without them
41	> every invocation fails with `Launching child process failed`. `--cap-add
42	> NET_ADMIN` + `--device /dev/net/tun` are needed for `network_mode: egress`
43	> functions. `docker compose up -d` (see [Install](#install)) sets all of this for you.
44	
45	Open **http://localhost:8443**, finish onboarding (~30s), and deploy your first
46	function from the in-browser editor.
47	
48	Prefer Compose, a bare-metal service, or just the CLI? See **[Install](#install)**.
49	
50	---
51	
52	## Screenshots
53	
54	| | |
55	|---|---|
56	| **System overview** — live metrics, warm pools, latency percentiles | **Functions** — runtime, resources, last deploy |
57	| ![System Overview](docs/screenshots/system-overview-dashboard.jpeg) | ![Functions](docs/screenshots/functions-list.jpeg) |
58	| **Editor** — write, build, and test in the browser | **Traces** — causal waterfall across HTTP → F2F → jobs |
59	| ![Editor](docs/screenshots/function-editor.jpeg) | ![Traces](docs/screenshots/distributed-traces.jpeg) |
60	| **Activity** — live feed of API, CLI, MCP, and webhook events | **Invocation logs** — request, response, duration, trace link |
61	| ![Activity](docs/screenshots/activity-live-feed.jpeg) | ![Logs](docs/screenshots/invocation-logs.jpeg) |
62	| **API keys** — bearer tokens for CI, scripts, and agents | **Firewall & DNS** — per-function egress rules |
63	| ![API Keys](docs/screenshots/api-keys.jpeg) | ![Firewall](docs/screenshots/firewall-and-dns.jpeg) |
64	| **Built-in docs** — full reference at `/web/docs` | **Settings** — storage, OAuth apps, build info |
65	| ![Docs](docs/screenshots/built-in-docs.jpeg) | ![Settings](docs/screenshots/settings-oauth.jpeg) |
66	
67	---
68	
69	## Features
70	
71	- **Two runtimes** — `node` (Node.js 24, also runs TypeScript) and `python` (Python 3.14).
72	- **Real isolation** — every call runs in a fresh nsjail sandbox: user namespace, chroot, cgroup v2 limits, and a seccomp syscall allowlist. → [Security](docs/SECURITY.md)
73	- **Warm pools** — idle workers stay resident per function, so repeat calls skip cold start.
74	- **Built-in primitives** — per-function KV store, background jobs (retries + backoff), cron schedules, function-to-function calls, encrypted secrets, custom routes, and signed inbound webhooks.
75	- **Distributed tracing** — every HTTP → F2F → job chain shares one trace, with a waterfall view and zero code changes.
76	- **Versioning** — content-hashed deploys with one-click (or one-command) rollback and side-by-side diffs.
77	- **MCP + AI** — a 70-tool MCP server at `/mcp` and a built-in agentic AI assistant (dashboard or `orva chat`) that operate your instance with your own provider key. → [AI & MCP](#ai--mcp)
78	- **Templates** — 16 starters (Stripe/GitHub webhooks, JWT/OAuth, CSV→JSON, URL shortener, …) in the editor.
79	
80	---
81	
82	## Write a function
83	
84	The `orva` SDK is preinstalled in every sandbox — KV, function-to-function invoke, and
85	background jobs with no setup:
86	
87	```js
88	// Node — Python uses the same shape: from orva import kv, invoke, jobs
89	const { kv, invoke, jobs } = require('orva')
90	
91	exports.handler = async (event) => {
92	  await kv.put('hits', (await kv.get('hits') || 0) + 1)
93	  await invoke('send-notification', { msg: 'hello' })   // child span in the same trace
94	  await jobs.enqueue('audit-log', { at: Date.now() })   // async, retried on failure
95	  return { statusCode: 200, body: { ok: true } }
96	}
97	```
98	
99	Handler contract, event shape, and streaming: [docs/RUNTIMES.md](docs/RUNTIMES.md).
100	
101	---
102	
103	## Install
104	
105	**Docker Compose** (recommended for persistent setups):
106	
107	```bash
108	curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/main/docker-compose.yml -o docker-compose.yml
109	docker compose up -d
110	```
111	
112	**Bare-metal / VM** — systemd or OpenRC, no Docker (Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora/RHEL/Rocky/Alma, Alpine, Arch, openSUSE):
113	
114	```bash
115	curl -fsSL https://github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
116	```
117	
118	**CLI only** — operator laptop or CI runner (Linux, macOS, Windows × amd64/arm64):
119	
120	```bash
121	curl -fsSL https://github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/releases/latest/download/install-cli.sh | sh   # macOS / Linux
122	irm  https://github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva/releases/latest/download/install-cli.ps1 | iex        # Windows
123	```
124	
125	Installers are idempotent — re-run to upgrade; pin a version with `ORVA_VERSION=vYYYY.MM.DD`.
126	TLS, reverse proxy, and backup guidance: [docs/DEPLOYMENT.md](docs/DEPLOYMENT.md).
127	
128	---
129	
130	## CLI
131	
132	The same binary is server **and** client. After `orva login`, the whole platform is in your terminal:
133	
134	```bash
135	orva deploy ./src --name my-fn --runtime node   # runtimes: node | python
136	orva invoke my-fn --body '{"name":"world"}'
137	orva logs my-fn --follow
138	orva chat                                        # the AI assistant, in your terminal
139	```
140	
141	Output is scripting-clean (`-o json`; data on stdout, status on stderr). Full reference: [docs/CLI.md](docs/CLI.md).
142	
143	---
144	
145	## AI & MCP
146	
147	Add Orva to any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, or claude.ai via OAuth) with one URL:
148	
149	```
150	https://your-orva-instance/mcp
151	```
152	
153	The agent can create and deploy functions, invoke them, read logs, manage secrets, and browse KV.
154	Prefer not to wire up an external client? The dashboard's **AI** section — and `orva chat` — run
155	the same agent in-product with your own provider key (OpenAI, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible
156	endpoint) and optional per-write approval.
157	
158	---
159	
160	## Configuration
161	
162	Defaults work out of the box. Common knobs: `ORVA_PORT` (8443), `ORVA_DATA_DIR`
163	(`/var/lib/orva`), `ORVA_SECURE_COOKIES` (set `true` behind HTTPS). Full reference:
164	[docs/CONFIG.md](docs/CONFIG.md).
165	
166	---
167	
168	## Documentation
169	
170	| | |
171	|---|---|
172	| [ARCHITECTURE](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) | System design, request + deploy lifecycle |
173	| [SECURITY](docs/SECURITY.md) | Threat model, sandbox isolation, verification recipe |
174	| [RUNTIMES](docs/RUNTIMES.md) | Handler contract, event shape, streaming |
175	| [API](docs/API.md) | Full REST API reference |
176	| [CLI](docs/CLI.md) | Config precedence, command reference, workflows |
177	| [CONFIG](docs/CONFIG.md) | All configuration knobs |
178	| [DEPLOYMENT](docs/DEPLOYMENT.md) | TLS, reverse proxy, backups, upgrades |
179	| [OPERATIONS](docs/OPERATIONS.md) | Monitoring, troubleshooting, common errors |
180	| [SUPPORT](docs/SUPPORT.md) | Distro / kernel / container-runtime matrix |
181	| [CAPACITY](docs/CAPACITY.md) | Throughput numbers + benchmark methodology |
182	| [CONTRIBUTING](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) | Dev setup, build from source, tests |
183	
184	Runtime isolation specifics (Kata, gVisor) live in [docs/KATA.md](docs/KATA.md) and [docs/GVISOR.md](docs/GVISOR.md).

3	# Fast PR / push gate. Owns ALL shell linting for the repo so the heavier
4	# install-e2e + cli-e2e workflows don't have to re-lint the same scripts.
5	# Path-filtered: docs-only / screenshot-only commits skip CI entirely.
6	
7	on:

11	      - '**.md'
12	      - 'docs/screenshots/**'

30	  lint:
31	    name: shellcheck (all)
32	    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
33	    steps:
34	      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
35	
36	      - run: sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends dash shellcheck
37	
38	      # POSIX scripts (install.sh, install-cli.sh) MUST run under any POSIX sh
39	      # on user systems. dash -n catches bashisms that shellcheck -s sh would
40	      # also catch; running both keeps the gate tight. install.sh embeds the
41	      # systemd/OpenRC units + uninstall.sh as heredocs, so there is no
42	      # standalone uninstall.sh to lint here.
43	      - name: POSIX user-facing scripts

46	          dash -n scripts/install-cli.sh
47	          shellcheck -s sh -S warning \
48	            scripts/install.sh \
49	            scripts/install-cli.sh
50	
51	      # bash scripts — entrypoint + test/install/* + test/cli/*. Failing
52	      # builds here gate the install-e2e + cli-e2e workflows downstream.
53	      - name: bash scripts
54	        run: |
55	          bash -n scripts/entrypoint.sh
56	          bash -n scripts/build-rootfs.sh

59	            scripts/build-rootfs.sh \
60	            test/install/*.sh \
61	            test/install/lib/*.sh \
62	            test/cli/*.sh \

67	    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

     3	# End-to-end verification of the standalone Orva CLI.
     4	#
     5	# Shell linting lives in ci.yml (one source of truth across the repo).
     6	# Go unit tests + cross-build + Linux installer test run on every CLI
     7	# push. The expensive runners (macOS + Windows) only fire when the
     8	# installer scripts themselves change, or on schedule, or on manual

    10	
    11	# Least-privilege default token (these jobs only read the repo).
    12	permissions:
    13	  contents: read
    14	
    15	on:
    16	  # Source validation (unit + cross-build) runs on PRs. The install jobs
    17	  # download the RELEASED CLI, so they run on release:published (against the
    18	  # freshly-published artifacts) — not on main-push, which would race the
    19	  # release cut and 404 on "latest".
    20	  release:
    21	    types: [published]
    22	  pull_request:
    23	    paths:
    24	      - "cli/**"
    25	      - "internal/client/**"
    26	      - "internal/ids/**"
    27	      - "scripts/install-cli.sh"
    28	      - "scripts/install-cli.ps1"
    29	      - "test/cli/**"

    34	    # and gives the expensive macOS/Windows jobs a guaranteed run.
    35	    - cron: "0 4 * * 0"

    38	  # Detect whether this run actually touched the installer scripts.

    40	  # minutes on every CLI code change.
    41	  changes:
    42	    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    43	    outputs:

    45	    steps:

    62	      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6

   175	          & $exe --version
   176	          # Confirm slim CLI lacks `serve`.
   177	          $serveOut = & $exe serve --help 2>&1
   178	          if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) {
   179	            throw "slim CLI on Windows unexpectedly has 'serve' subcommand"
   180	          }
   181	          Write-Host "OK: slim CLI on Windows correctly lacks 'serve'"
   182	          # Confirm completion script generation works.
   183	          & $exe completion powershell | Out-File -FilePath "$env:RUNNER_TEMP\orva-completion.ps1"
   184	          if ((Get-Item "$env:RUNNER_TEMP\orva-completion.ps1").Length -lt 100) {
   185	            throw "completion script too small — likely failed"
   186	          }
   187	
   188	  upgrade:
   189	    name: orva upgrade round-trip
   190	    needs: [install-linux]
   191	    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
   192	    env:
   193	      GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
   194	    steps:
   195	      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
   196	      - name: install jq + curl

   198	      - name: run upgrade-test.sh

     1	name: install-e2e
     2	
     3	# Real install + smoke + uninstall across 6 distros, in privileged
     4	# systemd-in-docker containers. The cheap stuff (shellcheck on the
     5	# install scripts themselves) lives in ci.yml — this workflow assumes
     6	# the scripts pass lint and focuses on actually running them.
     7	
     8	# Least-privilege default token (these jobs only read the repo).
     9	permissions:
    10	  contents: read
    11	
    12	on:
    13	  # Runs AFTER a release publishes — these download the released binary, so
    14	  # they must not run on main-push: during a release cut the old release is
    15	  # already gone and the new one isn't published yet, so "latest" 404s. On
    16	  # release:published they validate the freshly-published artifacts.
    17	  release:
    18	    types: [published]
    19	  pull_request:
    20	    paths:
    21	      - "scripts/install.sh"
    22	      - "scripts/uninstall.sh"
    23	      - "test/install/**"
    24	      - ".github/workflows/install-e2e.yml"
    25	  workflow_dispatch: {}
    26	  schedule:
    27	    # Weekly Sunday 03:00 UTC catches rolling-release breakage (Arch).
    28	    - cron: "0 3 * * 0"
    29	
    30	jobs:
    31	  matrix:
    32	    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    33	    # Two distros are advisory rather than gating:
    34	    #   arch   — rolling release; pacman mirrors drift between runs and
    35	    #            occasionally serve stale signatures or 404 individual
    36	    #            versions, so a transient mirror flake shouldn't block.
    37	    #   alpine — musl + glibc-built nsjail works via gcompat for the
    38	    #            install + smoke flow, but openrc's reinstall edge case
    39	    #            (uninstall then immediate reinstall + service start)
    40	    #            occasionally races on the GH runner. Smoke flow proves
    41	    #            the core install works; the reinstall round-trip is a
    42	    #            nice-to-have we'll harden later.
    43	    continue-on-error: ${{ matrix.distro == 'arch' || matrix.distro == 'alpine321' }}
    44	    strategy:
    45	      fail-fast: false
    46	      matrix:
    47	        distro:
    48	          - ubuntu24
    49	          - debian12
    50	          - alpine321
    51	          - rocky9
    52	          - fedora41
    53	          - arch
    54	    steps:
    55	      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
    56	
    57	      - name: Install jq + curl
    58	        run: |
    59	          sudo apt-get update -qq
    60	          sudo apt-get install -y jq curl
    61	
    62	      - name: Run install + smoke + uninstall for ${{ matrix.distro }}
    63	        # ORVA_BROWSER_LEG=0 skips agent-browser in CI (no display).
    64	        # HTTP route spot-checks still run.
    65	        env:
    66	          ORVA_BROWSER_LEG: "0"
    67	        run: bash test/install/run-distro.sh ${{ matrix.distro }}
    68	
    69	      - name: Upload logs
    70	        if: always()
    71	        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
    72	        with:
    73	          name: install-e2e-${{ matrix.distro }}
    74	          path: |

════════════════════════ .github/workflows/cleanup-ghcr.yml ════════════════════════
     1	name: cleanup-ghcr
     2	
     3	# Manual one-shot prune of accumulated old versions in
     4	# ghcr.io/harsh-2002/orva. The release workflow's cleanup-ghcr job
     5	# already does this automatically on every tag push — this standalone
     6	# workflow exists so an operator can prune NOW without re-running the
     7	# full ~15-min release pipeline (when, for example, prior releases
     8	# left orphan versions behind before the cleanup job existed).
     9	#
    10	# Trigger from the Actions tab → "cleanup-ghcr" → "Run workflow".
    11	# Optional `tag` input picks which release's manifest to preserve;
    12	# defaults to whatever ghcr's :latest currently points at.
    13	
    14	on:
    15	  workflow_dispatch:
    16	    inputs:
    17	      tag:
    18	        description: "release tag to preserve (default: whatever :latest resolves to)"
    19	        required: false
    20	        default: ""
    21	
    22	permissions:
    23	  packages: write
    24	
    25	jobs:
    26	  prune:
    27	    name: prune old ghcr versions
    28	    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    29	    steps:
    30	      - name: resolve target tag
    31	        id: tag
    32	        env:
    33	          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    34	          INPUT_TAG: ${{ github.event.inputs.tag }}
    35	        run: |
    36	          if [ -n "$INPUT_TAG" ]; then
    37	            echo "tag=$INPUT_TAG" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    38	            exit 0
    39	          fi
    40	          # Resolve :latest → digest → find the tag that shares that digest.
    41	          latest_digest=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/harsh-2002/orva:latest --raw \
    42	            | sha256sum | awk '{print "sha256:"$1}')
    43	          # The :latest manifest itself is a multi-arch manifest list. Find
    44	          # which version row in the API has 'latest' in its tags — that
    45	          # row's adjacent tag (vYYYY.MM.DD) is what we preserve.
    46	          tag=$(gh api -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github+json' \
    47	            "/users/Harsh-2002/packages/container/orva/versions?per_page=100" \
    48	            --paginate \
    49	            --jq '.[] | select(.metadata.container.tags // [] | index("latest")) | .metadata.container.tags[] | select(. != "latest")' \
    50	            | head -n1)
    51	          if [ -z "$tag" ]; then
    52	            echo "::error::could not resolve a non-latest tag from the current :latest manifest"
    53	            exit 1
    54	          fi
    55	          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    56	          echo "::notice::resolved current release tag: $tag"
    57	
    58	      - name: prune everything that isn't $TAG
    59	        env:
    60	          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    61	          TAG: ${{ steps.tag.outputs.tag }}
    62	          PKG_OWNER: Harsh-2002
    63	          PKG_NAME: orva
    64	        run: |
    65	          set -eu
    66	
    67	          # Same logic as release.yml's cleanup-ghcr job. Resolve the
    68	          # digest tree of the current manifest, then delete anything
    69	          # not in that tree and not tagged with $TAG or 'latest'.
    70	          docker buildx imagetools inspect "ghcr.io/${PKG_OWNER}/${PKG_NAME}:${TAG}" --raw \
    71	            | jq -r '..|.digest? // empty' \
    72	            | sort -u > /tmp/keep_digests.txt
    73	          echo "Digests to keep:"
    74	          cat /tmp/keep_digests.txt
    75	
    76	          gh api -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github+json' \
    77	            "/users/${PKG_OWNER}/packages/container/${PKG_NAME}/versions?per_page=100" \
    78	            --paginate \
    79	            --jq '.[] | "\(.id)|\(.name)|\((.metadata.container.tags // []) | join(","))"' \
    80	            > /tmp/versions.txt
    81	
    82	          total=$(wc -l </tmp/versions.txt)
    83	          deleted=0
    84	          kept=0
    85	          echo "Inspecting $total total package versions:"
    86	
    87	          while IFS='|' read -r id sha tags; do
    88	            keep_reason=""
    89	            # 1. Keep if version carries the current tag or 'latest'.
    90	            if echo ",$tags," | grep -qE ",($TAG|latest),"; then
    91	              keep_reason="tag=$tags"
    92	            # 2. Keep if version's sha is referenced by the current manifest tree.
    93	            elif grep -qx "$sha" /tmp/keep_digests.txt; then
    94	              keep_reason="part of current $TAG manifest"
    95	            # 3. Keep all untagged versions. Multi-arch manifests reference
    96	            #    their per-arch sub-images by digest only — those show up as
    97	            #    untagged in the GHCR versions API. Deleting them breaks
    98	            #    `docker pull` on the parent manifest. The keep_digests
    99	            #    extraction is best-effort; this branch is the safety net.
   100	            elif [ -z "$tags" ]; then
   101	              keep_reason="untagged (likely a sub-image manifest)"
   102	            fi
   103	
   104	            if [ -n "$keep_reason" ]; then
   105	              echo "  keep   id=$id tags=$tags ($keep_reason)"
   106	              kept=$((kept+1))
   107	              continue
   108	            fi
   109	
   110	            echo "  delete id=$id tags=$tags"
   111	            if gh api -X DELETE \
   112	                -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github+json' \
   113	                "/users/${PKG_OWNER}/packages/container/${PKG_NAME}/versions/${id}" 2>/tmp/delete-err; then
   114	              deleted=$((deleted+1))
   115	            else
   116	              echo "::warning::failed to delete version $id: $(cat /tmp/delete-err)"
   117	            fi
   118	          done < /tmp/versions.txt
   119	
   120	          echo "::notice::cleanup-ghcr done — kept=$kept, deleted=$deleted, of $total total."
   121	          {
   122	            echo "## cleanup-ghcr summary"
   123	            echo ""
   124	            echo "- preserved tag: \`$TAG\` (+ \`latest\` + sub-images)"
   125	            echo "- kept: $kept versions"
   126	            echo "- deleted: $deleted versions"
   127	            echo "- total inspected: $total"
   128	          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

1	# Backend
2	
3	Go 1.26 (bumped from 1.25 — the embedded Bifrost AI gateway requires go ≥1.26; the Dockerfile + all CI workflows pin golang 1.26 in lock-step). Module: `github.com/Harsh-2002/Orva` (rooted at the repo, not at
4	`backend/`). SQLite with no CGO (`modernc.org/sqlite`).
5	
6	The server binary built from `backend/cmd/orva` is the daemon (`orva serve`)
7	plus all CLI subcommands. The CLI subcommands live at `cli/commands/`
8	(package `commands`) — `backend/cmd/orva/main.go` imports
9	`cli/commands` and calls `commands.NewRoot()` then bolts on its own
10	`serve` / `setup` / `init` constructors. Single source of truth for
11	every client subcommand; the slim standalone CLI at `cli/cmd/orva`
12	uses the same library.
13	
14	## Build & Test
15	
16	```bash
17	# From repo root:
18	make build          # → build/orva (server + CLI bundled)
19	make test           # go test ./...
20	make lint           # go vet ./...
21	
22	# Direct invocations (also from repo root, since go.mod is here):
23	go build ./backend/cmd/orva
24	go test ./...
25	go vet ./...
26	```
27	
28	## Package Layout (`internal/`)
29	
30	| Package | Purpose |
31	|---|---|
32	| `config` | Config struct; env var + YAML loading |
33	| `database` | SQLite schema, migrations, all CRUD helpers |
34	| `registry` | In-memory function registry wrapping DB |
35	| `builder` | Deploy pipeline: tarball → `npm install` / `pip install` → optional `tsc` → register |
36	| `pool` | Warm-sandbox pool manager (`pool.Manager`) per function |
37	| `sandbox` | nsjail process lifecycle; `Worker` type with `Dispatch`/`DispatchEx` |
38	| `proxy` | HTTP → sandbox bridge; request capture (A3); streaming write-loop (C1) |
39	| `metrics` | Prometheus-text counters + histograms (no external deps, atomic ops) |
40	| `secrets` | AES-256-GCM encrypted secrets per function |
41	| `scheduler` | Cron runner (`robfig/cron/v3`) |
42	| `mcp` | MCP server (go-sdk); 70 operator-management tools OR channel-mode (one tool per bundled function, invoke-only). Auth accepts API keys, OAuth 2.1 access tokens, OR channel tokens. |
43	| `oauth` | OAuth 2.1 authorization server (RFC 7591 DCR + RFC 8414 metadata + PKCE S256 + RFC 8707 resource indicators + RFC 7009 revocation). Lets claude.ai/ChatGPT add `/mcp` as a custom connector via the browser. Connected apps + sessions managed at `/api/v1/oauth/connected-apps` and `/api/v1/auth/sessions` and surfaced in the dashboard's Settings page. DCR default scope is `read invoke write admin`. |
44	| `auth` | Shared `Principal` type (Kind=api_key / oauth / channel + ID/Label/Perms/Channel). Both REST middleware and MCP auth resolve the inbound bearer to a `*Principal`; downstream code (activity log, MCP tool registration) consumes the Kind directly. |
45	| `trace` | Causal-trace collector + span lifecycle (W3C `traceparent` interop, outlier detection). See `docs/TRACING.md`. |
46	| `urlhint` | Per-request `BaseURL(r)` helper. One source of truth for OAuth issuer URLs, MCP `invoke_url` fields, and audience-bound token validation. |
47	
48	**Agent channels** — bundle N functions under a name + a static bearer token; presenting that token at `/mcp` exposes ONLY those functions as MCP tools (snake_case names, invoke-only). Operator-managed at `/api/v1/channels` (`Channels` page in the dashboard). Token format: `orva_chn_<32 hex>`. Channel tokens are explicitly rejected with 401 at `/api/v1/*` — they have no Orva-management authority.
49	| `firewall` | nftables outbound allow-list per function (lazy `sync.Once` probe) |
50	| `server` | HTTP router + middleware chain + all handlers |
51	| `server/events` | SSE event hub + outbound webhook fanout |
52	| `server/handlers` | One file per resource group; `respond/` sub-package |
53	| `cli` | Shared `Client` + `Config` for CLI subcommands |
54	| `backup` | `SnapshotDB` / `ArchiveTo` / `RestoreFrom` helpers |
55	| `version` | Single source of truth for the version string |
56	| `ai` | In-product AI chat assistant. `Manager` (service layer) wires the SQLite store, the secrets cipher (provider-key encryption), the in-process tool registry, the embedded Bifrost LLM gateway (`ai/llm`), and the agentic loop (`ai/agent`). Served at `/api/v1/ai/*` by `server/ai_handler.go` (SSE for chat/approval). The agent's `defaultSystemPrompt` const lives in `ai/manager.go` — it's a Go **raw string, so it must stay backtick-free** (escape any fenced-code examples by description, not literal ```). |
57	| `ai/llm` | Wraps the embedded Bifrost gateway (`github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core`) behind neutral types + a normalized event stream. `Account` resolves BYO keys from `ai_provider_configs` live. Thinking levels → `ChatReasoning`. |
58	| `ai/agent` | Agentic loop (≈25-iteration budget): stream model turn → emit SSE deltas → detect tool calls → approval-gate writes → in-process dispatch → feed results back. Decoupled from `mcp` (takes tools + a dispatcher). Two independent gates: the per-conversation **approval policy** (`all_writes` / `destructive_only` / `auto`, checked in `approvalNeeded`) and a separate code-enforced `confirm=true` requirement on destructive tools. |
59	
60	The canonical UUIDv7 generator (`ids`) and HTTP client (`client`) live at **repo-root** `internal/ids/` and `internal/client/` — shared with the slim CLI codebase, not under `backend/internal/`.
61	
62	## CLI Commands (`cmd/orva/`)
63	
64	All Cobra subcommands share one binary with the server. `orva serve` starts the daemon; every other command is a CLI client that reads `~/.orva/config.yaml`.
65	
66	Key files: `deploy.go`, `diff.go`, `functions.go`, `invoke.go`, `logs.go`, `cron.go`, `kv.go`, `jobs.go`, `secrets.go`, `webhooks.go`, `routes.go`, `keys.go`, `system.go`, `activity.go`, `completion.go`.
67	
68	## Key Patterns
69	
70	**Handler responses**: always use `respond.JSON(w, status, val)` / `respond.Error(w, status, "SLUG", "message")` from `server/handlers/respond/`.
71	
72	**Invocation funnel**: HTTP, cron, jobs, and F2F calls all go through `Worker.Dispatch()` (sync response) or `Worker.DispatchEx()` (multi-frame streaming). Never invoke nsjail directly from handlers.
73	
74	**Async DB writes**: execution rows use `database.AsyncInsertExecution*` batch writers — no synchronous DB calls on the hot proxy path.
75	
76	**Name resolution**: functions can be referenced by UUID or by name. Use `resolveFnID(db, nameOrID)` from `handlers/functions_helpers.go`.
77	
78	**Streaming wire protocol**: `response_start` → `chunk` (base64 body data) → `response_end` frames over the worker's stdin/stdout pipe. `proxy.Forward()` owns the write-loop.
79	
80	**Shared tool registry (single source of truth)**: every operator tool is declared once via `regAddTool` (`mcp/agent_registry.go`). That call registers the tool with BOTH the external MCP server (`server.go`, unchanged behavior) AND the in-process agent registry (`mcp.BuildAgentRegistry(deps, perms)`, gated to the principal's perms). The internal AI agent dispatches these tools directly as Go calls — no MCP transport, no HTTP. Same name/description/schema/destructive-hint feed both fronts, so they never drift. When adding a tool, use `regAddTool(rc, perm, def, handler)` inside a `register*Tools(rc *regCtx)` function — never bare `mcpsdk.AddTool`.
81	
82	## Middleware Chain
83	
84	`CORS → BodySizeLimit → Auth → RequestID → Logger → Handler`
85	
86	Auth middleware only runs on paths starting with `/api/`. Everything else (`/fn/`, `/metrics`, `/webhook/`, `/mcp`, custom routes) bypasses the API-key check entirely — per-function auth for invocations is enforced inside `InvokeHandler`. Internal SDK paths (`/api/v1/_kv/`, `/api/v1/_internal/`) use the per-process internal token instead of API keys.
87	
88	## Database
89	
90	SQLite WAL mode. All migrations in `internal/database/migrations.go` — additive only. `VACUUM INTO` produces consistent backup snapshots without a write lock.
91	
92	## Gotchas
93	
94	- `backend/cmd/orva/adapters/` is **generated** — edit `backend/runtimes/` instead; `make adapters-embed` syncs them.
95	- `execution_requests` has **no FK** to `executions` (intentionally dropped to fix async insert ordering); manual cascade runs in `DeleteExecution`.
96	- TypeScript deploys: after a successful `tsc`, the function's `Entrypoint` is updated to `dist/handler.js` in the DB. The validator on re-deploy checks for the source `.ts` file, not the compiled output.
97	- Zombie nsjail fix: `cmd.Wait()` is centralized in `Spawn` via `waitDone chan struct{}`; never call `Wait()` on the sandbox `cmd` anywhere else.
98	- **AI conversation editing is destructive-tail:** editing or deleting a chat message (`EditMessage` / `DeleteMessage` in `server/ai_handler.go`, backed by `database.DeleteMessagesFromSeq`) truncates the conversation at that message's `seq` — it deletes that message and every message + tool call after it, then (for edit) re-runs the turn. There is no branching history; the tail is gone. `Regenerate` is the same truncate-then-rerun on the last assistant turn.
99	- **AI turns are one-per-conversation:** the `ai.Manager` holds a keyed try-lock (`tryLockConv`/`unlockConv`) acquired by every mutating entry point (Chat, Resume, RegenerateLast, EditAndResend, DeleteMessageFrom). An overlapping turn on the same conversation is rejected — SSE `error` for streaming paths, `ai.ErrConversationBusy` → 409 for the JSON delete. `database.InsertMessage` assigns `seq` atomically inside the INSERT (`MAX(seq)+1` subquery); never split it back into a SELECT-then-INSERT.
100	- **AI gateway lifecycle:** `ai.Manager.Close()` releases the embedded Bifrost pools and is called from `Server.Shutdown` (via `s.router.ai`). The gateway is built lazily and rebuilt on provider-config change (`invalidateClient`).
101	- **Docs single source:** `docs/reference.md` is the canonical Orva reference markdown (~53 KB). `make docs-embed` syncs it to `backend/internal/mcp/reference.md` (embedded by the `get_orva_docs` MCP tool) and `frontend/public/docs.md` (served at `/docs.md` for the dashboard's Copy as Markdown button). Edit the canonical file then run `make docs-embed`; the Vue Docs page is the rendered version (separate templates) and must be updated alongside if content changes.
102

1	# Architecture
2	
3	Orva is a single-binary Go server (`orvad`) that fronts an HTTP API,
4	spawns nsjail-isolated workers per function, and serves a Vue
5	dashboard from the same port. SQLite is the only storage backend.
6	There is no separate control plane and no clustering — one host runs
7	the whole thing.
8	
9	## Component map
10	
11	What runs on the host:
12	
13	```
14	host kernel  (Linux ≥ 5.10, cgroup v2, unprivileged userns)
15	  │
16	  └─ orvad   (single Go process, listens on :8443)
17	       │
18	       ├─ HTTP server     /api  /web  /auth  /events (SSE)  /mcp
19	       ├─ Pool manager    per-function warm workers + KPA autoscaler
20	       ├─ Build queue     extract → install deps → atomic publish
21	       ├─ Event hub       SSE pub/sub for metrics + exec + deploy

69	## Process model
70	
71	Single Go process. No fork, no IPC for control flow — the autoscaler,
72	build queue, GC, and event hub all live as goroutines inside `orvad`.
73	
74	The only out-of-process work is **per-invocation nsjail spawn**:
75	`orvad` calls `nsjail` as a child, hands it the request frame on
76	stdin, reads the response frame from stdout, and reaps the child. The
77	nsjail child re-execs into the language runtime (`node` or `python3`)
78	with the chroot already set up.
79	
80	Per-function pools keep nsjail+adapter processes warm so subsequent
81	invocations skip the ~50ms spawn cost.
82	
83	## Request lifecycle (cold path)
84	
85	```
86	POST /fn/xxx/health
87	     │
88	     ▼ middleware: auth → rate-limit → CORS
89	     │
90	     ▼ InvokeHandler.ServeHTTP
91	     │
92	     ▼ Registry.Get(fnID)               ← in-memory cache, SQLite fallback
93	     │
94	     ▼ poolMgr.Acquire(fnID, ctx)       ← per-fn pool; autoscaler may spawn
95	     │      │
96	     │      ├ idle worker available?    → reuse
97	     │      └ no, total < dynamicMax?   → spawnFn(ctx)
98	     │             │
99	     │             └ sandbox.Spawn(cfg) → fork nsjail → rootfs chroot
100	     │                                                  → exec adapter
101	     ▼ proxy.Forward(worker, req)
102	     │      │
103	     │      ├ JSON-encode request frame
104	     │      ├ write to worker stdin
105	     │      ├ read response frame from worker stdout (with TimeoutMS)
106	     │      └ JSON-decode statusCode/headers/body
107	     │
108	     ▼ writeResponse(w, frame)
109	     │
110	     ▼ async-insert execution row       ← drained_loop in async.go batches writes
111	     │
112	     ▼ events.Hub.Publish("execution")  ← SSE subscribers see it live
113	     │
114	     ▼ poolMgr.Release(worker)          ← worker returns to idle channel
115	                                          (or killed if dynamicMax shrank)
116	```
117	
118	Warm path is identical except `Acquire` returns immediately from the
119	idle channel.
120	
121	## Deploy lifecycle
122	
123	```
124	POST /api/v1/functions/{id}/deploy-inline   {code, dependencies}
125	     │
126	     ▼ FunctionHandler.DeployInline
127	     │
128	     ├ tar+gz the inline code to /tmp/orva-inline-*.tar.gz
129	     │
130	     ▼ DB.InsertDeployment(status="queued", phase=null)
131	     │
132	     ▼ buildQueue.Submit(BuildJob{tarball, deploymentID})
133	     │
134	     ▼ (async) Queue.runJob in worker goroutine
135	     │      │
136	     │      ├ FnLock(fnID)              ← serializes against rollback
137	     │      ├ DB.UpdateDeploymentPhase("extract")
138	     │      ├ Builder.Build(ctx, fn, tarball)
139	     │      │     │
140	     │      │     ├ pre-flight statvfs check        → ErrInsufficientDisk
141	     │      │     ├ hashFile(tarball) → codeHash
142	     │      │     ├ if versions/<hash>/.orva-ready exists → cached short-circuit
143	     │      │     ├ scratch_dir = versions/<hash>.tmp.<rand>
144	     │      │     │     ├ extract tarball
145	     │      │     │     ├ ValidateArchive (reject path-traversal symlinks)
146	     │      │     │     ├ npm install / pip install (HOST-side, not in sandbox)
147	     │      │     │     ├ install adapter wrapper (main.js / main.py)
148	     │      │     │     └ touch .orva-ready
149	     │      │     └ atomic os.Rename(scratch_dir, versions/<hash>)
150	     │      │
151	     │      ├ DB.SetDeploymentCodeHash(deployID, codeHash)
152	     │      ├ Registry.Set(fn) with bumped version + hash
153	     │      ├ ActivateVersion(dataDir, fnID, codeHash)  ← symlink retarget
154	     │      ├ DB.FinishDeployment(succeeded)
155	     │      ├ events.Hub.Publish("deployment", {status:"succeeded", phase:"done"})
156	     │      └ poolMgr.RefreshForDeploy(fnID)  ← drains idle workers
157	     │
158	     ▼ next Acquire → spawnFn reads `current` symlink fresh → new code
159	```
160	
161	Symlink retarget is atomic (rename(2) on a symlink). nsjail binds the
162	symlink path itself (no deref at bind time), but reads-through happen
163	at exec time inside the new namespace, so workers that got their
164	`-R` mount before the swap continue serving the old code until they
165	exit. `RefreshForDeploy` drains the idle channel so the next spawn
166	picks up the new target.
167

170	```

176	├── functions/

179	│       └── versions/

191	
192	## Database schema
193	
194	One SQLite file, grouped by subsystem. Core tables:
195	
196	| table | what it stores |
197	|---|---|
198	| `users`              | onboarded admin/operator accounts |
199	| `sessions`           | UI cookie tokens (7-day TTL) |
200	| `api_keys`           | bearer tokens for `/api/v1/*` |
201	| `functions`          | name, runtime, current version + code_hash, status |
202	| `deployments`        | per-build audit trail (queued/building/succeeded/failed; rollback rows are source='rollback') |
203	| `executions` / `execution_requests` / `execution_logs` / `execution_log_entries` | every invocation + its captured request + stderr/stdout |
204	| `build_logs`         | stdout/stderr from `npm install` / `pip install` |
205	| `function_secrets`   | per-function encrypted env vars (AES-256-GCM) |
206	| `routes`             | custom URL → function-id mappings (`/webhooks/stripe`) |
207	| `pool_config`        | per-fn autoscaler tuning (min_warm, max_warm, target_concurrency) |
208	| `system_config`      | global tuning knobs (versions_to_keep, gc_interval_seconds, etc.) |
209	
210	Feature tables added since v0.2:
211	
212	| group | tables |
213	|---|---|
214	| Scheduling & queues  | `cron_schedules`, `jobs` |
215	| KV & fixtures        | `kv_store`, `fixtures` |
216	| Webhooks             | `event_subscriptions`, `webhook_deliveries`, `inbound_webhooks` |
217	| Tracing & activity   | `user_spans`, `activity_log` |
218	| Firewall             | `egress_blocklist` |
219	| Agent channels       | `channels`, `channel_functions` |
220	| OAuth 2.1            | `oauth_clients`, `oauth_authorization_codes`, `oauth_access_tokens` |
221	| AI assistant         | `ai_conversations`, `ai_messages`, `ai_tool_calls`, `ai_provider_configs`, `ai_settings` |
222	
223	Schema lives in [`backend/internal/database/migrations.go`](../backend/internal/database/migrations.go) (~34 tables).
224	Migrations are additive only — `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` + idempotent ALTER columns run on every boot. AI message/tool-call rows cascade-delete with their `ai_conversations` parent; editing or deleting a chat message truncates the conversation tail by `seq` (see `DeleteMessagesFromSeq`).
225	
226	## Component responsibilities
227	
228	### `backend/internal/server/`
229	
230	The HTTP layer. Routes, middleware, handlers, the SSE event hub.
231	Stateless — every request reaches into the pool manager, registry, or
232	DB for actual work.
233	
234	- `router.go` — `http.ServeMux` wiring, middleware chain
235	- `server.go` — `New()` constructs all subsystems and their cross-references
236	- `middleware.go` — request-id, body-size cap, CORS, logger
237	- `middleware_auth.go` — session cookie + API-key dispatch
238	- `events/` — SSE pub/sub broker (`hub.go`, `handler.go`)
239	- `handlers/` — one file per concern (functions, invoke, secrets, routes, etc.)
240	- `handlers/respond/` — error envelope helpers + `Retry-After` injection
241	
242	### `backend/internal/pool/`
243	
244	Warm worker pools, one per function, autoscaled.
245	
246	- `pool.go` — `Manager` owns a `sync.Map[fnID]*functionPool`
247	- `function_pool.go` — per-fn idle channel + acquire/release/sweep
248	- `autoscaler.go` — Knative-KPA-style: 60s stable + 6s panic windows, `dynamicMax` derived from CPU + memory budget
249	- `hostmem.go` — global memory budget tracker (refuses spawns past 80% reservation)
250	
251	### `backend/internal/sandbox/`
252	
253	nsjail invocation, per-spawn config, host-wide concurrency limiter.
254	
255	- `sandbox.go` — builds the nsjail argv (chroot, mounts, cgroup, seccomp)
256	- `worker.go` — JSON frame protocol over stdin/stdout, expiry tracking
257	- `seccomp.go` — Kafel policy (`default`, `strict`, `permissive`)
258	- `limiter.go` — host-wide `MaxConcurrent` semaphore with `TryAcquire`
259	
260	### `backend/internal/builder/`
261	
262	Build queue + version archive + GC + first-boot migration.
263	
264	- `queue.go` — bounded channel + `runtime.NumCPU()` worker goroutines
265	- `builder.go` — extract → validate → install deps → atomic publish
266	- `activate.go` — symlink retarget for both deploy and rollback
267	- `gc.go` — periodic prune of versions beyond `versions_to_keep`
268	- `migrate_fs.go` — one-shot upgrade of legacy `code/` dirs to `versions/<hash>/`
269	- `validator.go` — archive sanity (path traversal, runtime entrypoint check)
270	
271	### `backend/internal/database/`
272	
273	SQLite access. No ORM — explicit queries, prepared statements where
274	hot.
275	
276	- `migrations.go` — schema + idempotent ALTER loop
277	- `async.go` — batched-flush writer for executions (50-job batches or 50ms tick)
278	- One file per resource: `functions.go`, `deployments.go`, `secrets.go`, etc.
279	
280	### `backend/internal/proxy/`
281	
282	The bridge between HTTP and a sandbox worker.
283	
284	- `proxy.go` — encodes request as JSON frame, writes to worker stdin, reads response frame, propagates timeouts and errors
285	
286	### `backend/internal/registry/`
287	
288	In-memory function cache backed by SQLite. Hot path reads (every
289	invocation) avoid a DB round-trip.
290	
291	### `backend/internal/secrets/`
292	
293	Encrypts/decrypts per-function env vars. Master key is derived from
294	the data dir's existence; rotation is a future project.
295	
296	### `backend/internal/metrics/`
297	
298	In-memory ring buffer over the last ~8k invocations. Computes p50,
299	p95, p99 server-side so the dashboard doesn't recompute on every
300	poll.
301	
302	### `backend/internal/ai/`
303	
304	The in-product AI chat assistant — an agentic loop that operates the
305	instance end-to-end through the same tools the MCP server exposes, with
306	BYO provider keys. Served at `/api/v1/ai/*` (SSE for chat + approval).
307	
308	- `manager.go` — service layer: wires the SQLite chat store, the
309	  secrets cipher (provider-key encryption at rest), the in-process tool
310	  registry, the LLM gateway, and the agentic loop. Holds the agent's
311	  `defaultSystemPrompt` (a Go raw string — must stay backtick-free).
312	- `llm/` — wraps the **embedded Bifrost gateway**
313	  (`github.com/maximhq/bifrost/core`) behind neutral types + a
314	  normalized event stream. `Account` resolves BYO keys from
315	  `ai_provider_configs` at request time; thinking levels map to
316	  `ChatReasoning`. (The Bifrost dependency is why the module requires
317	  Go ≥1.26.)
318	- `agent/` — the agentic loop (≈25-iteration budget): stream a model
319	  turn → emit SSE deltas → detect tool calls → approval-gate writes →
320	  dispatch the tool **in-process as a Go call** (no MCP transport, no
321	  HTTP) → feed the result back. Decoupled from `mcp` — it takes a tool
322	  set + a dispatcher. Two independent gates protect mutations: the
323	  per-conversation approval policy (`all_writes` / `destructive_only` /
324	  `auto`) and a code-enforced `confirm=true` requirement on destructive
325	  tools.
326	
327	The tools the agent dispatches come from `mcp.BuildAgentRegistry`,
328	which is fed by the **same** `regAddTool` declarations that register
329	the external MCP server — one source of truth, gated to the principal's
330	perms, so the two fronts never drift. Served by
331	`backend/internal/server/ai_handler.go`; the dashboard surface is the
332	`AI` sidebar section (`frontend/src/views/AI.vue`).
333	
334	Concurrency + lifecycle invariants: every `/api/v1/ai/*` route requires
335	the `admin` permission; conversations are a shared operator space (not
336	isolated per credential). The manager serializes turns with a
337	per-conversation try-lock (overlapping turns are rejected, not
338	interleaved), `ai_messages.seq` is assigned atomically inside the
339	INSERT, and the LLM gateway is closed on `Server.Shutdown`.
340	
341	### `backend/runtimes/`
342	
343	Per-runtime adapter scripts. The adapter is the entrypoint nsjail
344	exec's into; it reads request frames from stdin, calls the user's
345	exported handler, and writes response frames back.
346	
347	- `node/adapter.js` — also used for node
348	- `python/adapter.py` — also used for python
349	
350	### `frontend/`
351	
352	Vue 3 + Pinia + Vite. Single-page dashboard served from `/web/` by the
353	Go server (the build output is embedded at compile time via
354	`//go:embed ui_dist`).
355	
356	- `src/views/` — one file per route (Dashboard, Editor, FunctionsList,
357	  Deployments, InvocationsLog, ApiKeys, CronJobs, Jobs, KVStore,
358	  Webhooks, InboundWebhooks, Channels, Firewall, Traces, TraceDetail,
359	  FunctionDiff, Settings, Docs, Onboarding, Login, and **AI** — the
360	  agentic chat)
361	- `src/stores/` — Pinia stores (`auth`, `system`, `events`, `confirm`,
362	  and `ai` — the chat timeline + streaming client)
363	- `src/components/common/` — shared primitives (`Modal`, `Drawer`,
364	  `Input`, `Button`, `IconButton`, `StatusBadge`, `ConfirmDialog`,
365	  `Toast`, …)
366	- `src/components/ai/` — the chat surface (composer, message list,
367	  tool-call cards, code/thinking blocks, provider settings)
368	- `src/api/` — axios client + endpoint helpers + EventSource wrapper.
369	  The AI chat is the exception: it streams over `fetch` +
370	  `ReadableStream` (the chat POST carries a body, so `EventSource`
371	  won't do)
372	
373	## Concurrency model
374	
375	Goroutines do almost everything. Critical concurrency primitives:
376	
377	- **Pool manager**: per-fn `sync.Map` lookup. Each function pool has a
378	  `chan *Worker` (buffered) for idle workers — Go channels handle the
379	  acquire/release synchronization.
380	- **Per-fn lock** (`Manager.FunctionLock`): serializes deploy and
381	  rollback on the same function. Different functions are independent.
382	- **Async writer**: single goroutine drains a `chan writeJob` and
383	  batches DB inserts. Replaces the old goroutine-per-call pattern that
384	  burned CPU at sustained 500+ req/s.
385	- **Autoscaler**: one goroutine per `Manager`, ticks every second,
386	  evaluates each function's pool against its EWMA stable + panic
387	  windows.
388	- **Reaper**: one goroutine per pool, sweeps idle workers past TTL.
389	- **GC**: one goroutine, prunes archived version dirs every 5 minutes.
390	- **Build queue**: `runtime.NumCPU()` worker goroutines drain a job
391	  channel.
392	- **Event hub**: subscribers each have a 32-deep buffered channel.
393	  Producers drop events for slow consumers rather than block.
394	
395	## Why these choices
396	
397	**Why a single binary?** Operational simplicity. One process to
398	upgrade, one log to tail, one volume to back up. We give up the option
399	of horizontal scaling — but the target is a self-hosted, single-host
400	deployment, where horizontal scaling is over-engineering.
401	
402	**Why SQLite?** The target is single-host. Postgres would force
403	operators to run two services and manage credentials between them. The
404	write rate is bounded by invocation throughput (one row per
405	invocation), and the async writer batches commits. SQLite in WAL mode
406	handles thousands of writes per second on commodity hardware.
407	
408	**Why nsjail per invocation?** Hardware isolation requires either
409	process-level (nsjail / gvisor / kata) or VM-level (firecracker)
410	sandboxing. nsjail is the cheapest — single fork + namespace setup,
411	no VM boot. Per-invocation isolation means a function compromise
412	cannot affect another function or the host. Warm pools amortize the
413	spawn cost.
414	
415	**Why Knative-style autoscaling?** Two-window EWMA (stable +
416	panic) handles bursty traffic gracefully. Stable smooths out transient
417	spikes; panic responds within seconds when sustained load arrives.
418	Combined with per-fn `dynamicMax` capped on CPU + memory budget, the
419	host stays healthy during traffic floods.
420	
421	**Why content-addressed deploys?** Identical redeploys are a no-op
422	(same hash → cached version dir). Rollback is a symlink retarget.
423	Garbage collection is "delete versions not in the keep window." The
424	alternative — re-extract and re-install on every redeploy — is
425	slower and provides no rollback story.
426	
427	## Reading order for new contributors
428	
429	1. `backend/cmd/orva/serve.go` — entrypoint; see how everything wires up
430	2. `backend/internal/server/server.go::New` — main constructor
431	3. `backend/internal/server/handlers/invoke.go` — hot path (HTTP → pool → sandbox)
432	4. `backend/internal/pool/pool.go::Manager` + `function_pool.go::acquire` — the warm-pool dance
433	5. `backend/internal/builder/builder.go::Build` + `activate.go::ActivateVersion` — deploy + rollback
434	6. `frontend/src/stores/events.js` + `frontend/src/views/Dashboard.vue` — SSE consumption

361	// DispatchEx writes a request frame, reads the FIRST response frame, and
362	// dispatches by frame type:
363	//
364	//   - "response"        → DispatchResult{Streaming:false} populated end-to-end
365	//   - "response_start"  → DispatchResult{Streaming:true}; caller drives
366	//     NextFrame until kind=="end"
367	//
368	// On protocol errors the worker is marked dead. Worker.mu is held until
369	// the streaming caller finishes the loop (DispatchEx releases it inside
370	// NextFrame's terminal cases via finished=true; non-streaming returns
371	// release the lock immediately). This matches the contract that one
372	// Worker handles one request at a time.
373	//
374	// NOTE: holding w.mu across the streaming loop is fine because the pool
375	// guarantees a single goroutine owns each Worker, and Release happens
376	// after the proxy's Forward unwinds.
377	func (w *Worker) DispatchEx(ctx context.Context, eventJSON []byte) (*DispatchResult, error) {
378		if w.dead.Load() {
379			return nil, errors.New("worker dead")
380		}
381		w.mu.Lock()
382		// We can't unconditionally defer Unlock here because streaming holds
383		// the lock until NextFrame finishes. Both terminal paths (non-stream
384		// + stream-end + error) take responsibility for unlocking.
385		unlocked := false
386		unlock := func() {
387			if !unlocked {
388				unlocked = true
389				w.mu.Unlock()
390			}
391		}
392	
393		if w.dead.Load() {
394			unlock()
395			return nil, errors.New("worker dead")
396		}
397	
398		errBefore := w.errBuf.Len()
399	
400		// Compose the request frame: {"type":"request","event":<raw>}.
401		reqFrame, _ := json.Marshal(frameRequest{Type: "request", Event: json.RawMessage(eventJSON)})
402	
403		// Wire write must complete or we bail.
404		writeErrCh := make(chan error, 1)
405		go func() {
406			writeErrCh <- writeFrame(w.stdin, reqFrame)
407		}()
408	
409		// Read FIRST response frame on another goroutine so ctx cancel can
410		// break us out.
411		respCh := make(chan []byte, 1)
412		readErrCh := make(chan error, 1)
413		go func() {
414			payload, err := readFrame(w.stdout)
415			if err != nil {
416				readErrCh <- err
417				return
418			}
419			respCh <- payload
420		}()
421	
422		select {
423		case err := <-writeErrCh:
424			if err != nil {
425				w.markDead()
426				unlock()
427				return &DispatchResult{w: w, errBefore: errBefore},
428					fmt.Errorf("%w: write frame: %v", ErrWorkerExited, err)
429			}
430		case <-ctx.Done():
431			w.markDead()
432			unlock()
433			return &DispatchResult{w: w, errBefore: errBefore}, ctx.Err()
434		}
435	
436		select {
437		case payload := <-respCh:
438			var resp frameResponse
439			if err := json.Unmarshal(payload, &resp); err != nil {
440				w.markDead()
441				unlock()
442				return &DispatchResult{w: w, errBefore: errBefore},
443					fmt.Errorf("%w: invalid response frame: %v", ErrWorkerExited, err)
444			}
445			if resp.Type == "error" {
446				if resp.Fatal {
447					w.markDead()
448					unlock()
449					return &DispatchResult{w: w, errBefore: errBefore},
450						fmt.Errorf("%w: adapter fatal: %s", ErrWorkerExited, resp.Message)
451				}
452				// Non-fatal adapter error: handler threw but VM is healthy. Do
453				// NOT mark dead; do NOT classify as ErrWorkerExited.
454				unlock()
455				return &DispatchResult{w: w, errBefore: errBefore},
456					fmt.Errorf("adapter: %s", resp.Message)
457			}
458			if resp.Type == "response" {
459				// Non-streaming back-compat path: full response in one frame.
460				w.Served.Add(1)
461				unlock()
462				return &DispatchResult{
463					Streaming:  false,
464					StatusCode: resp.StatusCode,
465					Headers:    resp.Headers,
466					Body:       resp.Body,
467					w:          w,
468					errBefore:  errBefore,
469					finished:   true,
470				}, nil
471			}
472			if resp.Type == "response_start" {
473				// Streaming: keep the lock — the caller drives NextFrame and
474				// unlocks via the wrapper below when finished.
475				r := &DispatchResult{
476					Streaming:  true,
477					StatusCode: resp.StatusCode,
478					Headers:    resp.Headers,
479					w:          w,

483				// achieve this by replacing the helper closure ... but Go

509	// Quit sends a clean shutdown frame, waits grace, then SIGTERMs, then SIGKILLs.
510	//
511	// All synchronization with the underlying process happens via w.waitDone,
512	// which the single Wait() goroutine launched in Spawn closes once the PID
513	// has been reaped. Quit MUST NOT call cmd.Wait() itself — doing so races

515	// which would silently leave nsjail unreaped.

517		if w.dead.Load() {
518			return w.Kill()
519		}
520		quitFrame, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"type": "quit"})
521		_ = writeFrame(w.stdin, quitFrame)
522		_ = w.stdin.Close()

524		select {

527			return nil

529		}

532		if w.Cmd.Process != nil {
533			_ = w.Cmd.Process.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM)
534		}
535		select {
536		case <-w.waitDone:
537		case <-time.After(grace):
538			_ = w.Kill()
539			// Wait briefly for the Spawn-side reaper to finish so the caller
540			// returning from Quit can rely on the process being gone. Bounded
541			// so a wedged kernel can't hang shutdown forever.
542			select {
543			case <-w.waitDone:
544			case <-time.After(grace):
545			}
546		}
547		w.markDead()
548		return nil
549	}
550	
551	// Kill is an immediate SIGKILL of the worker's process group.
552	//
553	// Reaping is owned by the single Wait() goroutine launched in Spawn — we
554	// must NOT call cmd.Wait() here. Calling Wait() twice on the same
555	// *exec.Cmd is a documented race that can leave nsjail unreaped (the
556	// loser sees "Wait was already called" and returns without reaping).
557	// Pre-fix this was the path that produced <defunct> nsjail entries after
558	// streaming-client disconnects: markDead → pool kill → duplicate Wait.
559	func (w *Worker) Kill() error {
560		w.markDead()
561		if w.Cmd == nil || w.Cmd.Process == nil {
562			return nil
563		}
564		// Signal the whole process group (Setpgid=true at Spawn).
565		_ = syscall.Kill(-w.Cmd.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGKILL)
566		_ = w.Cmd.Process.Kill()
567		// The Spawn-side reaper goroutine will pick up the SIGKILL exit and
568		// close waitDone. Caller does not block on it — w.Kill returns as soon
569		// as the signal is delivered.
570		return nil
571	}

573	// IsDead reports whether the worker has been marked unusable.
574	func (w *Worker) IsDead() bool { return w.dead.Load() }

577	func (w *Worker) GetCgroupPath() string {
578		w.cgroupPathMu.Lock()
579		defer w.cgroupPathMu.Unlock()
580		return w.CgroupPath
581	}

583	// IsExpired reports whether the worker should be retired based on age or
584	// use count. Either zero disables that check.
585	func (w *Worker) IsExpired(ttl time.Duration, maxUses int64) bool {
586		if ttl > 0 && time.Since(w.Spawned) > ttl {
587			return true
588		}
589		if maxUses > 0 && w.Served.Load() >= maxUses {
590			return true
591		}
592		return false
593	}

595	func (w *Worker) markDead() {
596		w.dead.Store(true)
597		// Close stdin so a blocked read on the adapter side unblocks and exits.
598		_ = w.stdin.Close()
599	}

601	// ── Framing helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
602	
603	func writeFrame(w io.Writer, payload []byte) error {
604		var hdr [4]byte
605		binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(hdr[:], uint32(len(payload)))
606		if _, err := w.Write(hdr[:]); err != nil {
607			return err
608		}
609		if _, err := w.Write(payload); err != nil {
610			return err
611		}
612		return nil
613	}
614	
615	func readFrame(r io.Reader) ([]byte, error) {
616		var hdr [4]byte
617		if _, err := io.ReadFull(r, hdr[:]); err != nil {
618			return nil, err
619		}
620		n := binary.BigEndian.Uint32(hdr[:])
621		if n == 0 {
622			return []byte("{}"), nil
623		}
624		if n > 64*1024*1024 { // sanity cap — 64 MB per frame
625			return nil, fmt.Errorf("frame too large: %d bytes", n)
626		}
627		buf := make([]byte, n)
628		if _, err := io.ReadFull(r, buf); err != nil {
629			return nil, err
630		}
631		return buf, nil
632	}
633	
634	// ── Stderr ring buffer ────────────────────────────────────────────────
635	
636	// ringBuffer is a fixed-size, write-only ring used to capture the last N
637	// bytes of stderr per worker. Reads are via Snapshot(from).
638	type ringBuffer struct {
639		mu      sync.Mutex
640		buf     []byte
641		size    int
642		written int64 // total bytes ever written
643	}
644	
645	func newRingBuffer(size int) *ringBuffer {
646		return &ringBuffer{buf: make([]byte, size), size: size}
647	}
648	
649	func (r *ringBuffer) Write(p []byte) (int, error) {
650		r.mu.Lock()
651		defer r.mu.Unlock()
652		for _, b := range p {
653			r.buf[int(r.written)%r.size] = b
654			r.written++
655		}
656		return len(p), nil
657	}
658	
659	// Len returns the cumulative byte count (monotonically increasing).
660	func (r *ringBuffer) Len() int64 {
661		r.mu.Lock()
662		defer r.mu.Unlock()
663		return r.written
664	}
665	
666	// Snapshot returns the bytes written since the 'from' marker. If the
667	// buffer wrapped past that point, the oldest overwritten bytes are lost.
668	func (r *ringBuffer) Snapshot(from int64) []byte {
669		r.mu.Lock()
670		defer r.mu.Unlock()
671		if r.written <= from {
672			return nil
673		}
674		want := int(r.written - from)
675		if want > r.size {
676			want = r.size
677		}
678		start := int(r.written-int64(want)) % r.size
679		out := make([]byte, want)
680		if start+want <= r.size {
681			copy(out, r.buf[start:start+want])
682		} else {
683			n := copy(out, r.buf[start:])
684			copy(out[n:], r.buf[:want-n])
685		}
686		return out
687	}

45	// ServeHTTP is the hot path for function invocation. It accepts two path
46	// shapes:
47	//   - /fn/{id}/... — direct invoke (id is the short form without "fn_" prefix)
48	//   - any custom route previously registered via /api/v1/routes that maps
49	//     a user-chosen path (e.g. /webhooks/stripe) to a function_id
50	func (h *InvokeHandler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
51		reqID := r.Header.Get("X-Request-ID")
52	
53		var fnID string
54		// Prefix we should strip from the incoming request path before handing
55		// it to the sandboxed function. For /fn/{id} this is handled inside
56		// proxy.Forward; for custom routes we compute the strip here based on
57		// whether the match was exact or a `/prefix/*` match.
58		var stripPrefix string
59	
60		// Check custom routes first. MatchRoute tries exact match, then the
61		// longest `/prefix/*` match.
62		if route, matched, err := h.DB.MatchRoute(r.URL.Path); err == nil && route != nil {
63			if route.Methods != "*" && route.Methods != "" {
64				allowed := false
65				for _, m := range strings.Split(route.Methods, ",") {
66					if strings.EqualFold(strings.TrimSpace(m), r.Method) {
67						allowed = true
68						break
69					}
70				}
71				if !allowed {
72					respond.Error(w, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed, "METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED",
73						"method not allowed for this route", reqID)
74					return
75				}
76			}
77			fnID = route.FunctionID
78			// For exact-match routes the function sees "/" as its path. For
79			// prefix routes it sees the sub-path after the prefix so its
80			// internal router (FastAPI/Express/etc.) can dispatch.
81			if strings.HasSuffix(route.Path, "/*") {
82				stripPrefix = matched // e.g. "/shortener/"
83			} else {
84				stripPrefix = matched // full path → function sees "/"
85			}
86		} else {
87			// Fall back to /fn/{id} extraction.
88			fnID = extractFnID(r.URL.Path)
89		}

91		if fnID == "" {

93			return
94		}

100			return

103		// Status gate:
104		// - "active": proceed normally.
105		// - "building" AND a prior code directory exists: serve with the old
106		//   code (zero-downtime redeploy). This is the Heroku/Vercel model.
107		// - "building" with no prior code, or any other non-active status:
108		//   respond 503 with Retry-After so clients can poll.
109		if fn.Status != "active" {

112				// old code dir. Fresh deploys won't hit this branch because
113				// there's no prior code yet.
114			} else {

116				code := "NOT_ACTIVE"
117				msg := fmt.Sprintf("function status is %q, must be active", fn.Status)
118				if fn.Status == "building" {

136		// Per-function rate limit. perMin == 0 short-circuits inside Allow.
137		if fn.RateLimitPerMin > 0 {

145		}

148		// time naturally (the highest-volume table benefits most from
149		// time-clustered B-tree inserts).

259		execStatus := "success"
260		if result.StatusCode >= 500 {

262		}
263		h.DB.AsyncInsertExecutionFinal(
264			&database.Execution{

270		)
271		if h.Metrics != nil {
272			h.Metrics.Baselines.FinalizeExecution(h.DB, execID, fn.ID, execStatus, result.ColdStart, duration.Milliseconds())
273		}
274		// Persist stderr after the execution row so the FK constraint is satisfied.
275		if len(result.Stderr) > 0 {
276			h.DB.AsyncInsertExecutionLog(&database.ExecutionLog{

278				Stderr:      string(result.Stderr),

285	// UI panels (Dashboard recent invocations, InvocationsLog) prepend the
286	// new row without polling. The payload mirrors the Execution shape the
287	// list endpoint already returns.
288	func (h *InvokeHandler) publishExecution(id string, fn *database.Function, status string, statusCode int, durationMS int64, responseSize int, coldStart bool) {
289		if h.PublishEvent == nil {
290			return
291		}
292		now := time.Now().UTC()
293		h.PublishEvent("execution", map[string]any{
294			"id":            id,
295			"function_id":   fn.ID,
296			"function_name": fn.Name,
297			"status":        status,
298			"status_code":   statusCode,
299			"duration_ms":   durationMS,
300			"response_size": responseSize,
301			"cold_start":    coldStart,
302			"started_at":    now.Format(time.RFC3339Nano),
303			"finished_at":   now.Format(time.RFC3339Nano),
304		})
305	}

307	// hasPriorCode returns true if the function has a built code directory from
308	// a previous successful deploy. Used during redeploys so live traffic keeps
309	// hitting the old code until the new build succeeds.
310	func hasPriorCode(dataDir, fnID string) bool {
311		if dataDir == "" {
312			return false
313		}
314		st, err := os.Stat(dataDir + "/functions/" + fnID + "/code")
315		return err == nil && st.IsDir()
316	}

318	// extractFnID pulls the function ID from paths like /fn/{id} or
319	// /fn/{id}/sub/path. With UUIDv7 IDs, the URL form and the DB form are
320	// identical — no prefix-stripping or re-adding.
321	func extractFnID(path string) string {
322		const prefix = "/fn/"
323		if !strings.HasPrefix(path, prefix) {
324			return ""
325		}
326		remainder := strings.TrimPrefix(path, prefix)
327		if idx := strings.Index(remainder, "/"); idx >= 0 {
328			return remainder[:idx]
329		}

    14	// The link target is a relative path ("versions/<hash>") so the same
    15	// symlink resolves correctly if the data directory is moved or if the
    16	// container's mountpoint changes. nsjail does not deref symlinks at the
    17	// bind-mount source — `-R cfg.CodeDir:/code` binds the symlink path
    18	// itself — but the spawn closure resolves the link fresh on each Spawn,
    19	// so RefreshForDeploy draining workers is sufficient for the next spawn
    20	// to pick up the new target.
    21	func ActivateVersion(dataDir, fnID, codeHash string) error {
    22		if codeHash == "" {
    23			return fmt.Errorf("activate: empty code hash")
    24		}
    25		// codeHash becomes part of a filesystem path (versions/<hash>); it is
    26		// always a sha256 hex digest. Reject anything else defensively so a
    27		// traversal value can never reach the symlink target.
    28		if !isHexHash(codeHash) {
    29			return fmt.Errorf("activate: invalid code hash %q", codeHash)
    30		}
    31		fnDir := filepath.Join(dataDir, "functions", fnID)
    32		target := filepath.Join("versions", codeHash) // relative; see comment above
    33	
    34		tmp := filepath.Join(fnDir, "current.tmp."+randSuffix())
    35		if err := os.Symlink(target, tmp); err != nil {
    36			return fmt.Errorf("activate: symlink: %w", err)
    37		}
    38		current := filepath.Join(fnDir, "current")
    39		if err := os.Rename(tmp, current); err != nil {
    40			// Best-effort cleanup of the tmp link so we don't leave debris.
    41			_ = os.Remove(tmp)
    42			return fmt.Errorf("activate: atomic rename: %w", err)
    43		}
    44		return nil
    45	}
    46	
    47	// isHexHash reports whether s is a 64-char lowercase-hex sha256 digest.
    48	func isHexHash(s string) bool {
    49		if len(s) != 64 {
    50			return false
    51		}
    52		for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
    53			c := s[i]
    54			if !((c >= '0' && c <= '9') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'f')) {
    55				return false
    56			}
    57		}
    58		return true
    59	}
    60	
    61	// ResolveActiveHash reads `<dataDir>/functions/<fnID>/current` and returns
    62	// the hash it points at, or "" if the symlink is missing or malformed.
    63	// Used by GC to know which version not to delete.
    64	func ResolveActiveHash(dataDir, fnID string) string {
    65		link, err := os.Readlink(filepath.Join(dataDir, "functions", fnID, "current"))
    66		if err != nil {
    67			return ""
    68		}
    69		// Expecting "versions/<hash>"; strip the prefix.
    70		dir, hash := filepath.Split(link)
    71		if filepath.Clean(dir) != "versions" {
    72			return ""
    73		}
    74		return hash
    75	}

1	# Security model
2	
3	This document explains how Orva isolates user-supplied code from the host
4	and from other functions. It is descriptive, not prescriptive — every
5	claim below is grounded in a specific file/line that you can audit.
6	
7	## Threat model
8	
9	Orva is **single-tenant**: one operator, many functions, possibly many
10	end-users hitting those functions. The platform's security goals,
11	ordered by importance:
12	
13	1. A function cannot read or write **another function's data**
14	2. A function cannot read or write the **host filesystem** outside its
15	   own `/code` mount and its private `/tmp`
16	3. A function cannot **escalate to host root**, even though it appears to
17	   run as UID 0 inside its sandbox (more on this below)
18	4. A function cannot **exhaust host resources** beyond its declared
19	   memory / CPU / pid limits
20	5. A function cannot make **arbitrary network calls** when network mode
21	   is `none` (default — isolated net namespace, loopback only). Functions
22	   that need outbound HTTPS opt in by setting `network_mode: egress`
23	
24	Orva is **not** designed to defend against:
25	- A malicious operator running on the same host (they own the keys)
26	- A kernel-level zero-day (no seccomp filter is bulletproof against
27	  kernel exploits — see `nsjail` upstream's stance)
28	- Side-channel attacks (Spectre / Rowhammer / cache timing) — these are
29	  out of scope for any container-grade isolation
30	
31	## What's between user code and the host
32	
33	```
34	host kernel
35	  └─ docker container "orva"             ← UID 0 inside container; needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN
36	      └─ orvad (Go server)                  to construct sandboxes
37	          └─ nsjail process                ← unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) drops effective caps
38	              └─ user namespace
39	                  ├─ chroot to runtime rootfs (read-only)
40	                  ├─ /code bind-mount     ← read-only, function-private
41	                  ├─ tmpfs /tmp           ← private, wiped on worker exit
42	                  ├─ cgroup v2: memory + CPU + pids
43	                  ├─ seccomp filter       ← ~150 syscalls blocked
44	                  └─ user code (node / python)
45	```
46	
47	The gap between layers is enforced by the Linux kernel, not by Orva
48	code. Orva configures the boundaries and trusts the kernel to keep
49	them.
50	
51	## What "running as root inside the sandbox" actually means
52	
53	User code sees `getuid() == 0`. **It is NOT root on the host.**
54	
55	The mechanism is `CLONE_NEWUSER` + UID mapping. nsjail's `-Mo` flag
56	(`internal/sandbox/sandbox.go:154`) creates a new user namespace where
57	inside-UID 0 is mapped to host-UID 65534 (`nobody`). All capability
58	checks happen against the user-namespace's UID, but actions that cross
59	the namespace boundary (writing to a file owned by host-root,
60	mounting a filesystem outside the chroot, sending a signal to a host
61	PID) are denied because the function has zero effective capabilities
62	**outside** its namespace.
63	
64	Verify it yourself:
65	
66	```bash
67	# Deploy a fn that introspects /proc/self/status
68	KEY=$(docker exec orva cat /var/lib/orva/.admin-key)
69	
70	curl -X POST -H "X-Orva-API-Key: $KEY" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
71	  http://localhost:8443/api/v1/functions \
72	  -d '{"name":"whoami","runtime":"node","memory_mb":128,"cpus":1}'
73	
74	FID=$(curl -s -H "X-Orva-API-Key: $KEY" http://localhost:8443/api/v1/functions \
75	  | jq -r '.functions[] | select(.name=="whoami") | .id')
76	
77	curl -X POST -H "X-Orva-API-Key: $KEY" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
78	  http://localhost:8443/api/v1/functions/$FID/deploy-inline \
79	  -d '{"code":"const fs=require(\"fs\");module.exports=async()=>{return fs.readFileSync(\"/proc/self/status\",\"utf8\").split(\"\\n\").filter(l=>l.startsWith(\"Cap\")||l.startsWith(\"Uid\"));}"}'
80	
81	curl -X POST -H "X-Orva-API-Key: $KEY" \
82	  http://localhost:8443/fn/${FID} -d '{}'
83	```
84	
85	Expected output (the meaningful lines):
86	
87	```
88	Uid: 0  0  0  0
89	Gid: 0  0  0  0
90	CapInh: 0000000000000000      ← 0: no inheritable caps
91	CapPrm: 0000000000000000      ← 0: no permitted caps
92	CapEff: 0000000000000000      ← 0: no effective caps
93	CapBnd: 0000000000000000      ← 0: nothing in the bounding set
94	CapAmb: 0000000000000000      ← 0: nothing ambient
95	```
96	
97	UID 0 with **all 64 capability bits cleared**. The function can do
98	nothing root-on-the-host could do.
99	
100	## Filesystem isolation
101	
102	Configured at `internal/sandbox/sandbox.go:154-160`:
103	
104	```go
105	"-Mo",                          // mount mode: ownership-mapped userns
106	"--chroot", rootfs,             // pivot_root into the runtime's rootfs
107	"-R", cfg.CodeDir + ":/code",   // read-only bind mount of the function's code
108	"-T", "/tmp",                   // private tmpfs at /tmp
109	```
110	
111	- The runtime rootfs (`/var/lib/orva/rootfs/<runtime>/`) is the only
112	  filesystem visible. It contains the language runtime + standard libs.
113	- `/code` is a read-only bind mount of the function's code directory
114	  (`<dataDir>/functions/<id>/current` → symlink to `versions/<hash>/`).
115	  Read-only means the function cannot write back to its own code dir,
116	  which prevents persistent compromise of the deployment artifact.
117	- `/tmp` is a fresh tmpfs per spawn — wiped when the worker exits or is
118	  reaped. Functions can write here freely; nothing escapes.
119	- No other host paths are visible. The procfs, sysfs, and cgroup
120	  filesystems are masked by the chroot.
